utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed that there were preliminary matters to be raised. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I don't know if the Prosecution has anything preliminary but I have a preliminary matter to raise that pertains to GRM311 and the last bit of questioning from yesterday that, in fact, time-wise may have been the reason that we had to continue the witness today for ten to 15 minutes despite the efforts to finish the witness yesterday, including the request by VWS. Beginning at transcript page 22294, line 13 onwards, there are some considerable lapses in the translation that became evident from reviewing the videotape of yesterday's hearing, where the original B/C/S spoken by the witness does not correlate to the English that is a part of the transcript. We are mindful of how difficult a job it is to simultaneously translate, and indeed the translator said at transcript page 22295, lines 20 through 21: "The interpreter is not sure that the witness is clearly understood." There is apparent confusion seen from both the questions of Judges Moloto and Orie that appear to be the result of the incomplete and imprecise translation that we believe may have misled Your Honours. For purposes of correcting the record, the incidence at transcript page 22294, lines 13 through 19, the witness never mentioned headless bodies hanging from a church door but rather decapitated human heads. He never mentioned the hospital, he mentioned a factory. The fact that the driver claimed himself to be Serbian also is entirely missing from the transcript. Continuing at lines 19 through 25, the witnesses words are not entered when he said: "Going towards the factory, I came across an even greater horror where stray dogs, a pack of around 15 of them, were biting each other, and when I wanted to pass, three them had human heads tied around their necks and were fighting with one another to try and chew them. That was 27 April 1993. I came earlier, as I had been driven by that guy, and armed people at the gate would not let me inside. Rather, they made me go far away." This is significantly different from the English transcript. The words that Judge Orie asks about at transcript page 22295, lines 12 to 13: "They were biting them and biting off parts of their bodies," is not to be found in the B/C/S original of what the witness said. It is significant that neither in the English -- pardon me, neither in the B/C/S original does the witness ever say that he was running. That notion of running is for the first time raised by Judge Moloto's question at transcript page 22296, line 25, putting the words to the witness that he did not say. The Serbian word used by the witness in the first instance was "naletio sam." Judge Moloto's question as to running is translated to the witness in B/C/S as follows: [Interpretation] "That means that you were almost rushing along. You could move very fast, even though your leg was broken in this incident near the pit." [In English] The Serbian word --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, sorry to interrupt you. I suggest -- I have a suggestion, but I'd first like to briefly discuss it with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, the Chamber had some concerns that you are giving translations, but apart from that, the Chamber also understands your concerns.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether that is the most appropriate way of dealing with them is another matter. But the Chamber suggests the following, and would like to hear from the parties whether they would agree. First of all, that the yesterday's audio will be again interpreted and transcribed in full; second, that the witness will be asked to tell this part of his testimony, this piece of the story again, in detail, so that we have both a better insight in what may have gone wrong yesterday. And second, that we hear now the testimony of the witness in full on this incident. Mr. Ivetic, would that --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is in line with what we were intending to ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- insofar as we wanted the section from transcript pages 22294 through 22298, including both the B/C/S translated to the witness and the B/C/S spoken by the witness and the correct English equivalents of both to be redone by CLSS. So that would be in line with what Your Honours are suggesting, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. MacGregor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The Prosecution has no objection to the review and retranslation of the transcript excerpts. As to asking the same questions to the witness today, I'll defer to the Chamber. I would point out that the two particular issues that Mr. Ivetic has raised were actually corrected by the witness himself. The issue about headless bodies, eventually later in the transcript he corrected to say, no, it wasn't headless bodies, it was heads. And the question dealing with Judge Moloto's question about running, the witness himself said "to run into," is different. So I actually found that overall it was clear what the witness had said and he managed to correct that himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, the Chamber will invite the witness to tell the story again, and if any further unclarities remain, you still have an opportunity in re-examination to further clarify these matters. Since the parties seem to be in support of the suggested way to proceed, that's what we'll do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If I can request that it be done before I begin the rest of my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I wanted to -- yes, because if there is any confusion during cross-examination, you should have an opportunity to -- to further explore matters once they have been clarified. And to the extent they are not, Mr. Ivetic still has an opportunity to further seek clarification. Mr. Ivetic, any other matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, that is all that I had, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. MacGregor, I was informed that you had a question as well as.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mine are actually just about exhibits and administrative housekeeping, so I can deal with it as the witness is brought in if you would prefer to save time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, although it may take some time because we might need Madam Registrar to assign numbers, et cetera, and I'd rather avoid that the witness has to wait again. So let's first deal with those.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The first matter is yesterday we had Exhibit P6576 entered into evidence. This was the map zoomed in with the blue line drawn upon it. I've talked to the Registrar and I would like to have the map zoomed out without the line as a separate additional exhibit. My understanding is that's the only way to have both versions before the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And if you say the map without the line, you mean the blue line because the red lines were there already.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Correct. So the 65 ter of the original is 30766.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that original version with the red marking made in a previous case would receive number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30766 receives number P6578, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Yes, Ms. MacGregor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And my last, final issue. Yesterday you may remember that I put a question to the witness regarding enquiries that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: -- Prosecution made about his health records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Health records or enquiries about how his medical situation was perceived by coworkers?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: The enquiry was for that purpose but also to determine if there were any health records in the custody of his employer. The response that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Should we -- can we deal with it in open session?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: We can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: The response that we received is an internal OTP report describing the interview that was conducted. We are in the process of determining if we may seek to tender that into evidence and we'll have a determination by next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you shared it with the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I gave a copy to Mr. Ivetic yesterday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you postpone your determination whether or not you want to tender it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Yes, but I intend to give information to the Chamber by next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I can report that I received the English translation. I would like to see what the language is in the original and what the source is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I will do that very soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. And that will then be included in your submissions we could expect next week. Having said this, we have to turn briefly into closed session in order to have the witness be escorted in the courtroom. After that, we'll return into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning, Witness GRM311.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I first remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you have given at the beginning of your testimony, that you will tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Having said this, I would like to revisit a matter which was dealt with yesterday. Yesterday you have given testimony about an event which you described as starting with being taken into a black limousine, and what happened then, that is, about the dogs. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, there may have been some confusion about your testimony. There may have been some translation issues, and for that reason, I would ask you to tell us that part of the story again. And if you do that in small portions, then we may have some additional questions in order to avoid that further confusion would arise. So therefore, I would like to invite you to tell us again what happened when, as you said yesterday, you were stopped and you were taken into a black limousine. You said the men wouldn't stop, whereas you were supposed to get off, that part of the story. Could you please tell us that event again. So your limousine stopped, and could you tell us then what exactly happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only the driver was in the car. I said that he didn't wear a mask, he had a long beard, and his head was shaved. In front of the Novi Grad Municipal Assembly building or Assembly building, he opened the door and asked me, "Where are you going?" I said that I was going to work. He said to me, "Well, I can see that you're walking with difficulty and I'm going in the direction of the town. I can give you a lift." I told him that it was about a quarter past 5.00. I told him that I had plenty of time to get to the factory and to begin my work. Once again he said, "Get in, get in, I can give you a lift because I can see that you're walking with difficulty." We talked a little, he asked me where did I work, how many of you were there. It was obvious that he knew about my work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Please be cautious that if any part of the story, because you now started telling us a discussion about where you worked, that you do not reveal any deals such that someone would be able to identify you. So please be very cautious and ask for private session if you think you should tell us something that might reveal your identity. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Ms. MacGregor will now continue her cross-examination, Witness GRM311. Listen carefully to the questions and we'll try to keep it as short as possible. Ms. MacGregor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Good morning again, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: GRM311 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If I could please have Exhibit P6576 to not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to bring up again the map we were looking at yesterday, the map that has the red line showing your route from your home to Kosevo hospital. Now, when we're looking at the map, I'm going to ask you if you can see the railroad lines. They're shown as two black double lines pretty much parallel to the red line that you drew on the map. So once it comes up on your screen, we'll look for that line together. Okay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It takes a while to appear on your screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Okay. It seems to have come up now. If you look slightly above the red line, do you see the railroad track lines that I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: GRM311 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And just based on your knowledge of Sarajevo, are you familiar with the fact that there is a railroad line that runs along there?

utterances.speaker: GRM311 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I need to go into private session for one question please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, was there a road that ran -- is there a road that runs along the railroad tracks that we were just talking about?

utterances.speaker: GRM311 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, yes. It was built after the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I have one moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Now, if we can zoom out a little bit from this map right now. Just about one click.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Witness, do you see at the upper right-hand corner of this page there is a red rectangle along the railroad tracks which represents the train station?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And if it assists, perhaps we can zoom in on that particular quadrant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And if we look --

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Can I ask that we do zoom in a bit on that quadrant.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And if we look just under the railroad station, we see a road. It's very difficult to read, but the road is called Put Zivota, which is the "Route of Life." And do you know that street?

utterances.speaker: GRM311 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: You're not --

utterances.speaker: GRM311 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Put Zivota? I just heard that the Muslims proclaimed that. Now, why that was Put Zivota, the "Route of Life," I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: You're not aware that it was called that because it was an alternative safer route than walking along the Marshal Tito barracks along the red line that you have drawn on the map?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would object -- well, no, I withdraw my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. MacGregor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, my question was: You're not aware that this street was called the "Route of Life" because it was known as an alternative, safer route than the more dangerous route in front of the Marshal Tito barracks, you are unaware of that fact; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GRM311 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why that street was called that. I only heard of this name only after the war when I returned to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: GRM311 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to ask you, you've drawn on this map now --

utterances.speaker: GRM311 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: -- a red line and a blue line to show the route that you walked to get to Kosevo hospital. Now, you've just said that you regularly took a different route, Put Zivota, which you've not drawn as your route. Can you explain which of these routes did you regularly take?

utterances.speaker: GRM311 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took this road, by the railway station. I didn't draw this right because I can't see. This is the blue line that I drew yesterday, but I didn't draw it properly. I went further away from the railway station. Yes, this is where the railway station is. I think that this precisely is the railway station, this, and this is where I went. Along this route. The Marshal Tito barracks was a sort of shield there, and it went almost to Marin Dvor or to the mechanical engineering school or the technical school.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: When you've been saying "this," "this is the railway station," are you still referring to the red rectangular shape?

utterances.speaker: GRM311 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, are you aware that the route that is drawn in red on this map was known as sniper alley because of how dangerous it was during the war?

utterances.speaker: GRM311 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what it was called during the war. Even after the war I did not hear of that name. I know that sniper shooters were firing from the technical school, from the executive council building, and from two museums. All of that is there when you enter Marin Dvor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: We can remove the map from the screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you've given evidence that you walked along a route between your house and the Kosevo hospital once a week for nearly two years during the war. You testified that you walked past the PTT building, the Marshal Tito barracks, the Holiday Inn, the National Museum, the Assembly building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GRM311 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. I did not go by the Holiday Inn. I went along this route that I mentioned, by the railway station. Then I got into Kranjcevica Street where the military hospital is. And then along that street, next to the military hospital, I would go to the centre next to the Radnik cinema.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: You testified that when you walked, you never saw barricades or containers for civilians to hide in along the route. You also testified that throughout the entire war, from May 1992 until the middle of 1996, approximately four years, you testified that you never once saw UN personnel or UN vehicles in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GRM311 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I did see that but I don't remember seeing that, because there is nothing that would particularly attract me to that. Well, please, Muslims had tens of vehicles marked as UN in order to get closer to the Serbs to destroy them. The international community knows that but nobody reacted to that. The Muslims are now bragging about that in streets, in cafes, saying where they went and what they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Did you observe UN vehicles that were actually in the -- under the control of Muslims during the war?

utterances.speaker: GRM311 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see vehicles like that in anybody's hands. I heard people talking.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: So the information you just provided is based on something that you've heard either during the war or after the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GRM311 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I've already said I did not see that but I heard, even now, that they talk about that in public, that they camouflaged their own vehicles, their own tanks, painting the UN sign on them, in order to attack the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to you that your observations about what you saw in Sarajevo, especially your lack of ever seeing the presence of the UN during the war, that your observations about seeing mortars and artillery and snipers --

utterances.speaker: GRM311 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: GRM311 [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: -- I put it to you that your observations cannot be relied upon. It is simply beyond belief that you would not have seen the presence of the UN during the war. Do you have any explanation?

utterances.speaker: GRM311 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I wasn't interested in that. I was only interested in how I could get to work and how I could go back home and how I could do what I had been ordered to do. And what I saw, mortars, cannons, I had to see that because I passed by them just a metre or two away.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: You've also been inconsistent about the route that you took regularly between 1994 and 1996 to get from your house to the Kosevo hospital. Much of the route you've described would have been through one of the most dangerous, notorious thoroughfares in Sarajevo during the war, passing major military targets. This route, there is evidence that it was lined with barricades and containers in an attempt to protect civilians which you say you didn't see. You also claim you would have taken that route even though you were aware that there were safer routes to the north that you were aware of from where you worked. Now, this doesn't make sense to me that you would choose an unsafe route, especially as an injured man walking for two hours. Can you explain why you chose that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe, Your Honours, I would have to object to the question being compound, misstating what the witness actually said, relying upon uncited evidence or testifying. I mean, I can't tell the difference between it in the long, rambling question as it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. MacGregor, could you split up. And whenever you refer to the evidence of the witness, be precise on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I will try to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In addition to that, could you also refrain from any argumentative elements in your questions --

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm attempting, under Rule 90(H) --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not --

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: -- to make it clear what our position is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to explain why you put a question; I'm giving you guidance and instructions on how to put a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Excuse me for one moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours. I notice that this is also a time for a break. I think it's going to take me a bit of time to breakup this question efficiently, so I don't know if this is a good moment to take that break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take the break now. We have to move into closed session in order to allow the witness to leave the courtroom, and we'll resume in 20 minutes, again in closed session, and then turn into open session after that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Ms. MacGregor, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I'm going to take my questions a little slower. You've marked a route in red on a map to show how you walked to the Kosevo hospital, and you did that during your Dragomir Milosevic testimony; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GRM311 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may be so. However, I used the main road, and most of the time I used the route I yesterday marked in blue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Today you also mentioned a third route which included the road of Put Zivota; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I object. It misstates the evidence from yesterday, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I think that Ms. MacGregor was referring to today and --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's not different from yesterday, Your Honour. If you look --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- at the transcript at page 22306, the route described by the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so you would say --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- is that same route that we've talked about today. And at transcript page 22- --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but -- Mr. Ivetic --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can I make a record, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. It's clear what you meant when you said that -- as a matter of fact, you said it misstates the evidence from yesterday, whereas the question was about today --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Being different from yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay. I now understand that. I think Ms. MacGregor now also understands better the reference made by you. And it's my recollection that the witness explained a few things and, apart from all that, he said today that he's not very good at marking which may --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Which he also said yesterday when he marked it, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At transcript line [sic] 22307, 10 through 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. MacGregor, could you have a look at it and then again put your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Can I have one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it would take me a moment to study the transcript references Mr. Ivetic gave against the map, but I don't agree with the summary that Mr. Ivetic has given. My understanding of this witness's evidence is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're not, in the presence of the witness, discussing what it is. You'll have an opportunity to further look at it. If you put your next question to the witness, then you'll be given time to look at those pages and the Chamber will do the same. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I want it to be clear to you what the Prosecution position is on the evidence you've given about the route that you walked. What I'm putting to you is that the observations that you've conveyed about what you saw when you walked between your residence and the Kosevo hospital, that those observations are unreliable because you've been very inconsistent about where, in fact, you walked. Do you have any comment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it will be made. Mr. Ivetic, by the way, on page 22310, I think you referred to lines 7 to 12?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 22307, lines 10 through 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then I misheard. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to move on to a different topic. The medical care that you received at Kosevo hospital, did you ever receive treatment for your leg or your broken arm -- your broken arm or broken leg?

utterances.speaker: GRM311 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not during the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Today, Mr. Witness, when describing the incident with the man with the shaved head, you testified at transcript pages 14 to 17 of the temporary transcript, you testified that you believed he was trying to destabilise you psychologically. Now, did you feel psychologically destabled [sic] as a result of that incident and the other incidents you've talked about?

utterances.speaker: GRM311 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All Serbs who spent the war in Sarajevo were psychologically destabilised. If necessary, I can mention the names of those Serbs who were there during the war; although, I don't see them in Sarajevo itself as much or nearly as much as here in The Hague. All of them are destabilised. People walk about talking about things that simply don't exist. I know a case of someone who said that he was going to run for president. In other words, all of us were destabilised.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I want to ask you a few questions to follow up. So only Serbs who were in Sarajevo were psychologically destabilised? What about Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: GRM311 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can check that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: But what about your knowledge about Bosnian Muslims and what they suffered during the war?

utterances.speaker: GRM311 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did they discuss my life in Sarajevo during the war, the life that was imposed on me by them? Did you ever bother to check that, Madam Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: You've talked about many crimes that you saw committed against Serb civilians. I'm asking did you ever see or hear about crimes committed against Muslims civilians?

utterances.speaker: GRM311 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't discuss that. Until 1994, I was mostly in the factory, save for a few hours that I would get to spend home. In the evening when I did, they would call me three times per night to see whether I was there. When my wife answered, they wanted me on the phone personally. If I took -- when I took sick leave, the telephone was cut off immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: We don't have a lot of time, so I ask you, please, to listen to the questions I'm asking. Now you worked -- your two colleagues at the factory were Muslims; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GRM311 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: They never told you about crimes committed against Muslims that they heard about. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: GRM311 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no time to talk. 120 or 150 hand-grenades had to be made each day, and we did so without even as much as looking at each other, let alone talking.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: You were a civilian during the war; correct?

utterances.speaker: GRM311 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: You're not an expert on artillery; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GRM311 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I want to ask you a question about paragraph 15 of your statement. This is the paragraph where you describe how you got your daughter and your wife out of Sarajevo. The final sentence of that paragraph, you say: "Neither any of the international organisations nor UNPROFOR helped me to get members of my family out of the city." Now, you've said today that you did not see the presence of the UN in the city during the war, so why would you mention here in your statement that UNPROFOR did not assist you?

utterances.speaker: GRM311 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely because I didn't see them. I didn't know where they were to be found. I asked for help from the Muslims in my settlement. I asked for help from their command, but they wanted me to pay 5.000 German marks only for my daughter to come out of the town, and I didn't have that kind of money.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: So you did not approach UNPROFOR for assistance; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GRM311 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Turning to the incident again at the pit. Now, you've given evidence that as a result of that incident you broke your arm and your leg.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: That's at transcript 22261.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: You also gave evidence that you had fainting spells several times a day as a result.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: That's at 22288.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: You gave evidence that you continued to walk to work between January 1993 and June of 1994, a distance of 5 kilometres each way.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: This is at transcript 22280.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Today, you said you could barely walk from the same injury. Yesterday you mentioned not being able to walk at all during this period.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: That's at 22261.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: You gave evidence that you worked the same schedule 12 hours a day, seven days a week, at a physically demanding job.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: That's at transcript 22281 through 22283.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Additionally, your account of the incident at the pit has changed. On two occasions during your testimony in the Milosevic trial, you were recorded as saying that the incident occurred on the 27th of October 1992, and we discussed this yesterday at transcript 22285 through 86. You never once mentioned during the Milosevic trial that that incident occurred on Serb Christmas Eve. You confirmed that yesterday at transcript page 22286. Yesterday you said that the incident happened on 5 January 1993, and your explanation of why the dates were different from your Milosevic testimony is that somebody made a mistake, and that's at 22284. And I put it to you that your evidence that you've given about the pit, what you saw and what happened to you, is simply incredible based on the information I've just summarised. Do you have any explanation?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. You may proceed, Ms. MacGregor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Sir, you've claimed that you were abducted 11 times. This is in your statement -- 11 or 12 times, excuse me. Your statement at paragraph 7 and also at transcript page 22258. On the same transcript page, you claim that when you were abducted you were threatened every time. You testified that you never threatened to quit your job at the factory.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And that's at 22283.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: In fact, you also testified that the factory's own doctors recommended that you permanently leave the factory on -- excuse me, to go on sick leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And that's at 22290.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I have no doubt that you lived through traumatic events during the war. The Prosecution has no doubt about that. However, your testimony about being an eye-witness to murders, mutilated bodies, it has been inconsistent and incredible in the position of the Prosecution. Now, is it possible that these are not events that you yourself actually witnessed?

utterances.speaker: GRM311 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I said I said because I witnessed it. I didn't utter a single word that was not first-hand. If I -- if there was something that was not observed directly, I specified it to you example by example. But I will never forget what happened on the 5th of January, 1993, not because of the fact that my arm and leg were broken but because of all the psychological suffer I sustained. I began having fainting spells. I forgot about my arm and leg at the time, forgetting that it hurt, which is now coming back. I am paying for that now. As the Sarajevo physicians told me: Well, your injuries had not been treated and now you're facing those problems. However, the psychological problems are there to stay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. MacGregor. Before we give you an opportunity to re-examine the witness, Mr. Ivetic, Judge Fluegge would have a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we please have Exhibit D509, which is under seal, which should not be broadcast, and I'm referring to paragraph 16. That should be on the screen, please. And I want to read one sentence from your statement, Witness. In fact, two sentences at the end of paragraph 16. I think you see it on the screen. There I read, I quote: "Some pupils carried hand-grenades," and I leave out some words, "in their school bags. These pupils carried lists with the names and addresses of people at whom they were supposed to throw the hand-grenades that day." Can you explain where that happened? Where did you see these pupils and when did that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In December 1992, on my way out from the plant where I was working, my colleague was standing there, a Serb who worked there. He wasn't working on grenades. He was entrusted on preparations for processing. He was working with three boys of some 15 or 16 years of age. I don't know the exact date. Maybe it was the 2nd or the 3rd of December. And he said -- I mean, it's evident that he knew them, whose children they were, they knew their names. He said, "Here's the workman who does this," and they were curious. They stood around me. They were asking me questions and showing me that this is what they had in their bags, that these were casings made of thin tin and there were 12 grenades in there fixed so that they wouldn't shift. They showed me that each one of them had a paper stating where that day or that evening they were supposed to throw that grenade. They were carrying the paper with them. I didn't ask for it. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Witness, this concludes your testimony. I would like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again. Before you leave the courtroom, we'll briefly go into closed session and I already announce that we'll immediately also take a break and that we'll resume, and then, I think, in open session for the next witness, we'll resume at 20 minutes past 12.00. You may follow the usher after we have turned into closed session. We turn into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Defence ready to call its next witness? Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Stojanovic, no protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. None.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that sooner or later the report I think Mr. Weber started to give, that we'll hear from that soon? I didn't want to interrupt at that time the -- the testimony of the witness coming in.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. And if I -- I think he's already pointed it out, but a Google search of the hotel shows the hotel and the church next to it. So I think we'll agree on what the exhibit will be and we can tender that sometime next week. I think there are some other residual matters from that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct. And Mr. Weber has other duties this afternoon so we were going to meet to go over that at some later point, but we have located, with the name of the church, the physical address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, Mr. Mladic, no saluting when the witness comes in. You should refrain from that and you know it. Good afternoon, Mr. Andan, I take it. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Andan. Please be seated. Mr. Andan, you'll first be examined by Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic, and you noticed already that you find him to your left. You may proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Andan, I would like to ask you to state for the transcript your name and surname exactly.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: My name is Dragomir Andan.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you tell the Court whether at one point in time you gave a statement in writing to Mr. Mladic's Defence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes, I gave a statement in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please have document 65 ter 1D01602. Could we please have that in e-court. Also I would like us to take a look at the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, the information, the personal details on this page, are these details details that correspond to your own?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes, this is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And the signature on this page, is it your signature?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes, that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now take a look at the last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, when preparing for this testimony, did I give you an opportunity to look at your statement and did I give you this written statement consisting of a total of four pages?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We still have the first page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are still waiting for the B/C/S last page of the document. There we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to take a look at this statement? As stated here it has a total of three pages, and also is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes, I've had an opportunity of looking at this statement, and this is my signature and the date is the 8th of May, 2014.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today as I did during proofing and when we were preparing this statement, after having taken the solemn declaration in court today, would your answers be the same as the content of this statement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes, it would be identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please have Mr. Andan's statement admitted into evidence. It is marked 65 ter 1D01602.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I see two redactions in paragraph 12 and the Chamber is not used to receive statements with redactions. Now, I can imagine that you want to explain that not in open session, that's fine, but if we need to go into private session we -- we'd hear from you. But could you please explain. Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I may be able to assist in this matter. The two redactions -- there is two redactions and yet a third point in that paragraph where the witness's -- where the individual's name is listed in the paragraph, Mr. Zulic. We have been in touch with Mr. Zulic and he's advised that he would not require protective measures or redactions of the statement. His name is reflected in the paragraph but somewhat interestingly redacted [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it's all fine that you redact statements for the public, but for the Chamber not to know what is redacted is not what I expect. So this is the public version. And are you going to upload a version that should be admitted into evidence under seal, Mr. Stojanovic? Then we'll mark this version for identification and once the original version is uploaded, then we'll -- we'll then -- no, this one, of course, is not even marked for identification. We only need the unredacted one to be -- but we'll wait for you to upload it into the e-court system. If you would tell us, then we'll decide on admission, but as matters stand now there is -- the Chamber will admit the full version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Agreed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. With your leave, I would like to read out a brief summary of the statement of Mr. Andan. Witness Dragomir Andan spent most of his professional career in the police. When the war broke out, he was senior inspector first class in the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In June 1992, he was sent to carry out special tasks in order to deal with paramilitary formations in Brcko, Bijeljina, and Zvornik, which he carried out in co-operation with the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. From September 1992, he took a number of duties in the 65th Protection Regiment of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, where he stayed until September 1993 when he was transferred to the administration for intelligence and security of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. He took part in several military actions together with his unit, and he had the opportunity of meeting General Mladic several times and carrying out his direct orders. In his statement he speaks about how a senior police official was taken prisoner in Trnovo and he speaks about the personal attitude of General Mladic towards the status of this prisoner. As for another event which took place towards the end of 1993, when the VRS took prisoner several members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, at that moment General Mladic showed up in person and personally issued orders to send the POWs to the KP Dom Kula. And in accordance with rules on how POWs should be treated, he said that they should be exchanged, which was indeed done. The witness confirms that all units of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska always had strict orders to treat POWs in accordance with the Geneva Conventions. In the many military operations of which he had the opportunity of being close to General Mladic, he never heard an order that would have been against the Geneva Conventions, the rules and customs of war. Your Honour, I would like to just put a few more questions to the witness with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, could you please tell the Court when you had the opportunity of meeting General Mladic directly during the war? When did that happen for the first time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I first saw General Ratko Mladic in July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court where this took place?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: If you allow me, I would like to make a brief introduction, if that would be in line with my testimony in general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. You may answer the questions that Mr. Stojanovic puts to you, and if at the very end you think that an important matter has been missing, then you have an opportunity to correct that. But please focus on the questions that are put to you and answer them. The question was when -- can you tell the Court where you met him in July 1992 when you first saw him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Orie, this question requires a lengthier answer. It is within this question. I will try to be brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you first tell him where you saw him for the first time in July 1992. If Mr. Stojanovic has any follow-up questions, he'll ask them. But please give an answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Together with Mico Davidovic, who worked with me in Bijeljina, and we planned to carry out this operation in Zvornik, I saw --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No -- Mr. Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- General Mladic at the Main Staff --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. The simple question was where. Not with whom, nothing else. Where did you see him for the first time? When for the first time he appeared before your eyes. Please proceed and answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I first saw him in July 1992 at the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska in Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I'm going to ask you to tell the Court what the reason was. What was the reason for you to be at the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: After quite a few operative activities in the municipality of Zvornik and after having collected some intelligence, we came to the conclusion that the paramilitary formation of the Yellow Wasps should be eliminated. Our assessment was that the number of personnel that we had at that point in time, which was minimal, was such that we could not oppose a well-armed unit consisting of 120 men at the time. We did not know whether they belonged to the army, and Mr. Davidovic and I had a proposal to go to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska and to seek assistance from the intelligence people of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. Before that, Mr. Davidovic had reached a specific agreement with Mr. Salapura, and then the two of us went together to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska to spell out in concrete terms what we had precisely agreed upon before that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please slow down when speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please slow down because otherwise some of your words might be lost and we would like to hear them all. And could you make a small pause, Mr. Stojanovic, before putting the next question. And could you make a little pause when -- before answering the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, did you make a plan of activity together with the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska in relation to the disarming of paramilitaries in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We drew up our part of the plan. In agreement with representatives of the military security branch, we were supposed to work together on that plan to see to what extent they would be participating in that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you meet General Mladic on that occasion in person -- person on person, and what did you discuss?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes. At some point General Mladic entered the room where we were discussing our activities. He greeted us. And what I remember particularly was that when he shook our hands, he said, "Welcome to the club of honest men." Then he sat down and asked the two of us to brief him on the situation in the area that we covered operationally, which was Bijeljina, Zvornik, and Brcko. When we finished our presentation, he said that it was -- our greatest problem all over Republika Srpska was the fight against paramilitary formations and that we are unable to stabilise our confrontation line with the enemy until we have dealt with our paramilitary formations whose basic and only goal was to plunder and expel innocent Muslim civilians from the municipalities controlled by the Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please allow me to interject and put a question, for the record as well. With the exception of General Mladic, General Davidovic, and yourself, were there any other military personnel there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes, Colonel Salapura was there and the then Colonel Zdravko Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did General Mladic tell you anything else on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: He did say something that stayed with me for the rest of the war. He turned to the two of us and he said -- let me try to quote him exactly, he said that this was the most difficult war after the Second World War because of its nature and goals. He said that it was -- the most difficult the thing to do is to wage war against an enemy who speaks the same language and that it was a kind of civil war. He also said that what we needed to know was that we were not alone in that war. We all stopped for a few moments and then he continued. He said, "You must be aware that the entire world is following what we are doing here. You have to bear in mind that all people in your territory who are of Muslim or Croat ethnicity and who have not transgressed against the Serbian people must be protected. You need to bear in mind the Geneva Conventions and that it is also applied by everyone in Bosnia-Herzegovina and those monitoring the developments there."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I paused for the record. Given your professional career and your warpath, I wanted to ask you this: During the war, did you have occasion to see whether General Mladic abided by his words at any time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I believe I mentioned that in my statement. On several occasions I know he asked that the prisoners be put on a list, handed over to the military police, placed in gaol, and then exchanged for the same number of people of Serb ethnicity held by the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While you were engaged on intelligence tasks in the area of Sarajevo, did you have specific tasks received from General Mladic at any point in time concerning certain people?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes. It is something I will remember for the rest of my life. In 1995, maybe 15, 20, or 30 days after the signing of the Dayton Accords, I received information from my operatives to the extent that in Grbavica, which was an area covered by the VRS, that Christiane Amanpour was there, the CNN journalist, with her crew, interviewing military personnel and civilians there. I informed the assistant commander for intelligence and security in the SRK, Mr. Marko Lugonja, of that. I told him that there was a person of that profile in Grbavica. Quarter of an hour later Marko called me and, to use military parlance, he said that the boss ordered, and there he meant General Mladic, that I go down to Grbavica immediately in order to provide a secure environment for Ms. Amanpour, as he said, not a hair on her head was to be touched and she must leave Grbavica safely. My office was some 500 metres away from the centre of Grbavica, where she was. I left with several soldiers and I saw that some suspicious people were creating a circle around Ms. Amanpour. To be completely honest, Slavko Aleksic's Chetniks were the most active in that and they started insulting verbally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, although I've allowed it to continue for some time, all of this is new material which was not noticed to the Prosecution at any point. I would object --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I wouldn't say all of it but --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Almost all of it. The statement, the meeting with Mladic in July of 1992, what Mladic had to say to the witness in 1992 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, Ms. Bibles objects against going beyond what is presented in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is part of item 8 of this witness's statement, but now the witness is being more specific as to the topic he discussed there in terms of what tasks he was engaged in while being a part of the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you interpret paragraph 8 in this way, Mr. Stojanovic, there is no limit whatsoever to your examination. Certainly, I did not feel that a protection after the Dayton Agreement of journalists traveling around was an issue which is covered by paragraph 8. It's so vague that it doesn't even say within the war. Would you please focus on the most relevant issues and preferably closely linked to what we find in the statement. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall do so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, what year was that specifically?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me conclude this topic. Did you indeed carry out General Mladic's order as regards Ms. Amanpour?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes, I let her out of that group, provided her with a brief interview, and she safely went to the federation part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we next see P3802. Page 1 first.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, it is a report drafted by the Main Staff of the VRS. The date is the 28th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next, can we have the last page in both versions, where reference is made to an analysis of paramilitary formations in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The document was signed by the chief of the intelligence and security administration of the VRS Main Staff, Zdravko Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It reads: "The presence and activity of paramilitary formations negatively affect the Serbian people in two ways: (1) by diminishing trust in the government and its capacity to deal with war profiteers, criminals, and mass murderers; and (2), by immensely discouraging the fighting elan of SRBH Army members, often resulting in the abandonment of positions." In conclusion, the document reads: "Every armed Serb in SRBH must be placed under the exclusive command of the SRBH Army, or else he should be disarmed and legal measures taken." My question is this: Throughout the years of war and your efforts to deal with paramilitary formations, was this the position of the Main Staff of the VRS as specified in 1992? Was it seen through until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes, it was in place until the end of the war in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Andan. I conclude my questions and I hand you over to the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Ms. Bibles, are you ready?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, you'll now be cross-examined by Ms. Bibles. You'll find her to your right. Ms. Bibles is counsel for the Prosecution. You may proceed, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Andan.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, this is your third time testifying at ICTY. As I understand it, you testified for seven days during 2011 in the case of Stanisic/Zupljanin. And then when you testified in the Karadzic case, were you aware that much of your Stanisic/Zupljanin was used as your substantive testimony there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes, I was notified.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And today, as you understand it, your substantive testimony is the 20-paragraph statement that you've signed for the Mladic Defence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes, that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I noticed that you do not appear to have a copy of that statement with you. Would you like to have a copy as you're cross-examined? We can provide one.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could have the usher's assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's a clean copy, I take it --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- in -- in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, do you want to see it? You may give it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, because your experience, knowledge, in previous testimony covers additional details relevant to this case not fully captured in this statement, I'll be asking in a focused manner some of the additional details behind the 20 paragraphs. I have some questions first regarding your personal knowledge of Serbs setting up barricades in Sarajevo in March of 1992. You've previously testified that you weren't personally involved but that you were called in to two different events in which Serbs were involved in setting up barricades. Do you stand by that evidence today?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Please be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: You previously testified in Stanisic/Zupljanin, the transcript reference would be 21586, lines 6 through 20: "I cannot speak about things I haven't had personal involvement in, but there were two events when we were called up to come to the MUP and we learned that night that the Serbs were setting up barricades, that they wanted to separate Sarajevo or divide it into two parts. And the second event was when I went with Mr. Music, my colleague, to his house, where I saw a lot of armed men, but at that point in time and not even later, I have to say, did I realise that they were actually erecting barricades. I did see armed men. They were leaving their homes with long-barreled weapons. But at that point in time I wasn't aware that they were setting up barricades." Do you stand by that testimony?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I can confirm most of that testimony. I think in the latter part it didn't concern the setting up of barricades, when I went there with Mr. Music. As for the initial part, I decidedly said that as the senior inspector first class and a member of the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina, during the night we were called by the operations duty officer - and when I say "we," all of us active-duty inspectors - to come to the republican MUP. After a while, they told us that Serbs were erecting barricades in Vrbanja Most and in the direction of Pofalici. They also told us that we should be on the ready, those of us in the republican MUP. That is what I said and that is what I stand by. It is same event, Madam Prosecutor, because while waiting, although we were not addressed by any superiors, Mr. Teufik Music and myself set out at around 5 a.m. towards Bascarsija. He hails from there, and I was the chief of police there for four years. We went there to buy some bread so that we have something to eat. Then Teufik asked me to accompany him to Vratnik, which is in Stari Grad municipality, immediately next to Bascarsija. Then I saw those armed men leaving homes. They were Muslim. Previously, when we reached the city council building, we were stopped by a group of reserve policemen --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, I will ask you to be as focused as possible. I'll try to ask very focused questions to make that easier for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, before we continue. Witness, you said in the beginning of your last answer: "I can confirm most of that testimony. As for the rest of it, I respectively said that as the senior" -- and let me just see. Yes. "I think in the latter part it didn't concern the setting up of barricades, when I went there with Mr. Music." Now, do you say: I didn't say this about the barricades when I testified, in which case we'll just verify the words you have spoken. Or do you say: What I said at that time was unclear or not accurate or -- and you are changing it? Which of the two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understood the Prosecutor as saying that there were two types of barricades. I'm not disputing that Serbs set up barricades at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only thing Madam Prosecutor did was to quote, literally, what is recorded as your previous testimony. Now if you say: "As for the rest of it" -- no, no -- yes, "I respectively said that as the senior inspector" -- no, let me see. "I think in the latter part it didn't concern the setting up of barricades ..." Do you want to say: That's not what I said, as you read it to me? Or do you say: That's what I said but it was different? Which of the two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say that because that evening Muslims did not put up barricades. The Serbs put up barricades.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether you said it or not, you're saying the record of what you said in that other case is wrong. We'll then verify that, because the audio files are still existing and we'll just verify on the audio whether that is what you said or that you didn't say it. So therefore you say what Ms. Bibles read to you, and she reads from the official record, is not accurate, it doesn't reflect what I said. Do you understand your testimony well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, I'm going back to the second part. The first part that the Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- read is all right. As for the other part --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, it's a simple question. What Ms. Bibles read, do you challenge or do you dispute that that's what you said or do you say: No, that's what I said but it's -- I should clarify or change or whatever, it's not accurate. Which of the two? Did you -- what was read to you, did you say it in court at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say it like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's clarify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll verify what you said and how you said it and we might -- Ms. Bibles, you're invited to, with the assistance of -- I never know whether it's CMSS or the -- but to find the audio of that portion of the evidence so that it can be played to the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, would you agree of these individuals who were setting up barricades on the Serb side, that Momcilo Mandic was one of these individuals?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I would agree, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Would you agree that you have personal knowledge of his involvement in setting up barricades on the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Can you confirm that Mandic was with the police at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes, he was assistant minister for crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I next want to ask you about your reaction to the 31st March 1992 order that was sent out by Mandic setting up the creation of the Serbian police.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I won't pull it up but this is in evidence as P3009.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, you took this order from Mandic to a Sarajevo television station. Can you tell us, as briefly as possible, why?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I think that the translation was not correct. The order was last issued by Mladic, as it was translated to me in the first sentence. But the order -- or, actually, the dispatch was signed by Mr. Mandic. It is correct that I took the dispatch and took it to a journalist from Radio Television Bosnia-Herzegovina as an expression of revolt in relation to an order like that and the breakup of the integrity of the Bosnia-Herzegovina MUP. And it's correct that I did give that dispatch to the reporter.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And it's true that you were opposed to dividing the police based on ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Correct, yes, especially in view of the fact who were supposed to be the future leading figures of the police who wouldn't even know how to be at the head of the police service properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And do I understand correctly that you refused initially in April and May to join the Serbian police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Can you confirm that you were both encouraged by some and threatened by others about your decision in April and May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: It depends on the point of view. I was in the part of the Sarajevo that was still undivided. A number of my Muslim colleagues encouraged me and a number of Serbs with -- actually, about whom I tried to see who they were, where they stand, during the night they threatened me a couple of times and said that I should declare myself to be on the Serbian side. And because if I did not, something nasty would happen to me and they wouldn't be able to help me there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Without going into further details, did you eventually join the Serbian police by the 1st of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I did, yes. I don't know the precise date but I did join the police, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: When the Serbian MUP was formed, is it correct that -- well, the minister of the interior was Mico Stanisic. Was his deputy initially Momcilo Mandic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: As an inspector in the Serbian MUP, did you have a chain of command that culminated in Mico Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's the hierarchical chain where the minister is the number one person of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And in finishing this topic, I just want to ask whether the Serbian MUP had the authority, the legal authority to arrest active-duty VRS personnel?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Look, they could not arrest them from a formal legal aspect, but we did receive permission from the Main Staff that all those involved in illicit activities, regardless of whether they were soldiers or officers of the Army of Republika Srpska, were to be arrested and handed over to the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: We'll discuss some of those details later in your testimony. Next I would like to turn to some questions about your time in Brcko and Bijeljina from June to September of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, you are encouraged to show at least, even if you do not go into the details of a document, to at least -- in this case it was P3009, but to have it on the screen so that the Judges can at least read, even if you do not work on it in detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I appreciate the advice in that regard and I'll do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In paragraph 5 of your statement, you describe being sent to Brcko due to "problems that piled up in the presence of paramilitary formation." You were assigned to go to Brcko as an inspector. How long were you actually in Brcko as an inspector?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Two weeks at the most from what I can remember. Possibly three, but it was definitely not longer than three.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: You may not recall the exact date but did you arrive some time in early June 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I have a problem with dates. Please, don't take it ill. But I think it was in June. I'm not sure. I don't think that it was in early June. I think it was probably in the second half of June, but please, I -- don't ask me to give you the precise dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Whichever date it was, could you tell us whether law and order was present in Brcko when you arrived and -- and functioning in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Would you agree that there were no Muslim or Croat police officers remaining in Brcko when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. There were none left.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Is it true that the issue of looting and plunder committed by the paramilitaries was a major concern in Brcko when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, and that is the reason why I was sent to Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And is it true that Brcko is a rich area that has a port that brings items into the area, which is what enticed criminals to come loot and steal property in the Brcko area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
